336. What human beings regard as reasonable or unreasonable is not fixed. Certain epochs find reasonable what other epochs find unreasonable, and conversely.

Does this variation imply that reasonableness lacks objective character?

Consider that highly intelligent and well-educated persons believe the Biblical creation narrative, while others regard it as demonstrably false. The grounds invoked by the latter are not unknown to the former.

337. One cannot conduct experiments if some things are not left undoubted. This does not mean that one accepts certain presuppositions on trust. When I write a letter and post it, I take for granted that it will arrive—I expect this outcome.

When I perform an experiment, I do not doubt the existence of the apparatus before my eyes. I harbor many doubts, but not that one. When I perform a calculation, I believe without doubt that the figures on the paper are not switching of their own accord. I also trust my memory throughout, and I trust it without reservation. The certainty present here is of the same character as the certainty that I have never been on the moon.

338. Imagine persons who were never quite certain of these matters but said instead that they were very probably so, and that doubting them was not worth the effort. Such a person would say, in my situation, "It is extremely unlikely that I have ever been on the moon," and so forth. How would the lives of these persons differ from ours? There are persons who maintain that it is merely extremely probable that water over a fire will boil rather than freeze, and that therefore what we regard as impossible is, strictly speaking, only improbable. What difference does this make in their lives? Is it not simply that they speak rather more about certain matters than the rest of us?

339. Imagine someone who is to fetch a friend from the railway station. Rather than simply consulting the time-table and proceeding to the station at the right time, he says, "I have no belief that the train will really arrive, but I will go to the station all the same." He performs every action that the normal person performs, but accompanies it with doubt or with self-annoyance, and so forth.

340. We know, with the same certainty with which we believe any mathematical proposition, how the letters A and B are pronounced, what the color of human blood is called, that other human beings have blood and call it "blood."

341. Which is to say, the questions we raise and the doubts we entertain depend on the circumstance that some propositions are exempt from doubt—are, as it were, hinges on which those questions and doubts turn.

342. That is to say, it belongs to the logic of our scientific investigations that certain things are indeed not doubted.

343. The situation is not this: We simply cannot investigate everything and are therefore forced to rest content with assumption. If the door is to turn, the hinges must stay put.

The point is not that practical limitations compel us to accept certain things without investigation. Rather, the very possibility of investigation presupposes that certain matters are held fixed. The fixity of the hinges is not a concession to the impossibility of examining all things; it is a condition for the coherence of any examination whatsoever. If I attempt to investigate whether the hinges are secure while simultaneously treating the door's capacity to turn as an open question, I am not being more thorough—I am undermining the framework within which investigation operates.

344. My life consists in my being content to accept many things.

345. If I ask someone, "What color do you see at the moment?"—asking, that is, in order to learn what color is there at the moment—I cannot at the same time question whether the person I ask understands English, whether he intends to deceive me, whether my own memory is failing me with respect to the names of colors, and so on.

The question I pose has sense only given that these other matters are not in question. If I simultaneously doubt whether my interlocutor understands English, then my asking him a question in English becomes unintelligible as an attempt to learn anything. If I doubt whether my memory of color-names is reliable, then the answer I receive cannot inform me, since I cannot trust my understanding of that answer. The asking of the question thus presupposes a background of undoubted matters, not because I have investigated those matters and found them secure, but because their being held fixed is what makes the question itself coherent.

346. When I am trying to mate someone in chess, I cannot entertain doubts about the pieces perhaps changing places of themselves while my memory simultaneously plays tricks on me so that I fail to notice.

If these doubts were live, the activity I take myself to be engaged in—attempting to mate my opponent—would lose its sense. The game of chess presupposes that the pieces remain where they are placed unless moved by a player. If I doubt this, I am not playing chess more carefully; I am no longer playing chess.

347. "I know that that's a tree." Why does it strike me as if I did not understand the sentence, though it is an extremely simple sentence of the most ordinary kind? It is as if I could not focus my mind on any meaning, simply because I do not look for the focus where the meaning is. As soon as I think of an everyday use of the sentence instead of a philosophical one, its meaning becomes clear and ordinary.

The sentence seems empty or puzzling when considered in isolation from any context that would give it point. In everyday circumstances, the sentence has application: I might utter it to correct someone who mistakes the object for a shrub, or to confirm that my eyesight is functioning properly. Removed from such contexts, the sentence retains its grammatical form but loses its intelligibility. I seem not to understand it because there is, in the absence of context, nothing determinate to understand.

348. Just as the words "I am here" have meaning only in certain contexts and not when I say them to someone who is sitting in front of me and sees me clearly—not because they are superfluous, but because their meaning is not determined by the situation yet stands in need of such determination.

The sentence "I am here" is not rendered meaningful by the mere circumstance that I am indeed here. If I am standing before you and you see me plainly, my saying "I am here" does not communicate anything, not because what it says is too obvious to need saying, but because the situation does not confer on the sentence any determinate use. The sentence requires a context—I might utter it over the telephone, or to indicate my presence after having been called—that specifies what work it is to do. Without such context, the sentence is unmoored.

349. "I know that that's a tree" may mean all sorts of things. I look at a plant that I take for a young beech and that someone else thinks is a black-currant shrub. He says, "That is a shrub"; I say it is a tree. We see something in the mist which one of us takes for a man, and the other says, "I know that that's a tree." Someone wants to test my eyes, and so forth. Each time, the 'that' which I declare to be a tree is of a different kind.

Suppose we express ourselves more precisely, for example: "I know that that thing there is a tree; I can see it quite clearly." Let us even suppose I had made this remark in the context of a conversation, so that it was relevant when I made it. Now, out of all context, I repeat it while looking at the tree, and I add, "I mean these words as I did five minutes ago." If I added, for example, that I had been thinking of my bad eyes again and it was a kind of sigh, then there would be nothing puzzling about the remark.

For how a sentence is meant can be expressed by an expansion of it and may therefore be made part of it.

The sentence "I know that that's a tree" does not carry its meaning intrinsically. What I am doing in uttering it—whether correcting a misidentification, demonstrating the reliability of my vision, or something else—is not settled by the words alone. The meaning is fixed by the context, and when I specify that context (by explaining, for instance, that I am sighing over my poor eyesight), I thereby determine what the sentence is being used to say.

350. "I know that that's a tree" is something a philosopher might say to demonstrate to himself or to someone else that he knows something that is not a mathematical or logical truth. Similarly, someone who was entertaining the idea that he was no longer of any use might keep repeating to himself, "I can still do this and this and this." If such thoughts often possessed him, one would not be surprised if he, apparently out of all context, spoke such a sentence aloud. (But here I have already sketched a background, a surrounding, for this remark—that is to say, given it a context.) 

But if someone, in quite heterogeneous circumstances, called out with the most convincing mimicry, "Down with him!", one might say of these words (and their tone) that they constitute a pattern that does indeed have familiar applications, but that in this case it was not even clear what language the person in question was speaking. I might make with my hand the movement I should make if I were holding a hand-saw and sawing through a plank. Would one have any right to call this movement sawing, out of all context? (It might be something quite different!)

The philosopher's utterance "I know that that's a tree" is puzzling because the context—philosophical reflection—does not confer on it the sort of role it has in everyday circumstances. The philosopher is not correcting anyone, not confirming his eyesight, not doing any of the things for which the sentence ordinarily serves. He utters it as an example, to illustrate that empirical knowledge exists. But this use is parasitic on the sentence's ordinary applications, and when removed too far from those applications, the sentence becomes idle. It retains the appearance of meaningfulness without the substance.

Similarly, the person who keeps repeating "I can still do this and this" may be reassuring himself in the face of self-doubt. Here there is a context—a background of worry—that renders the repetition intelligible. But if someone utters words or makes gestures that, in some contexts, have familiar meanings, yet does so in circumstances that supply no such context, we are at a loss. The words and gestures are unanchored. They resemble language or purposeful action, but they are not, in these circumstances, instances of either.
